analysis.one_liner: Bans brand drug companies from paying generic competitors to keep cheaper drugs off the market.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in February 2012 with 6 Democratic cosponsors, was sent to two House committees and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: When a generic drug maker challenges a brand-name drug's patent, the two companies sometimes settle by having the brand company pay the generic maker to delay launching its cheaper version — a practice called "pay for delay." This bill would make those deals illegal, enforcing the ban through the Federal Trade Commission, with narrow exceptions for settlements that let the generic come to market early. It would also strip a generic maker's 180-day exclusivity reward if it struck a forbidden deal, and require drug companies to certify under penalty of perjury that they have disclosed the complete terms of any patent-settlement agreements to the FTC and Justice Department.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who fill prescriptions, and government programs like Medicare and Medicaid, would benefit because cheaper generic versions of drugs would reach the market years sooner. Generic drug makers would gain faster market access, though they would lose the cash settlements the bill bans. The FTC gains a clear enforcement tool against anticompetitive drug-company agreements.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unlawful unfair method of competition for a brand-name drug company to give anything of value to a generic applicant in exchange for an agreement not to research, develop, manufacture, market, or sell the generic drug [S3].

Treats violations as unfair or deceptive acts enforceable by the Federal Trade Commission under the Federal Trade Commission Act, while allowing the FTC to exempt by rule any settlement it finds pro-competitive and beneficial to consumers [S3].

Costs of delay fall on consumers, employers, and government insurers: the FTC has estimated pay-for-delay settlements add hundreds of millions of dollars a year to U.S. drug costs by keeping lower-priced generics off the market (widely reported agency and academic estimates; this bill was aimed squarely at that practice).

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would lose a tool for delaying generic competition and the extended periods of monopoly-priced sales it buys them. Generic drug makers would lose the value they currently receive for agreeing to stay off the market, and some patent disputes might be litigated to judgment rather than settled with side payments.

drawbacks.text: A near-blanket ban reaches some settlements that might be reasonable: the bill's exceptions cover only early generic entry or a waiver of past-damages claims, so settlements in which a generic maker accepts other value without pro-competitive terms would be prohibited even if a court might have found them lawful [S3].

Patent disputes are genuinely uncertain, and the risk that the challenger might lose is exactly what the value in a settlement can reflect; a per se ban removes that flexibility, though the FTC's rulemaking authority could soften this by exempting agreements found to benefit consumers [S3].
The bill forfeits a first generic filer's 180-day marketing exclusivity if it enters a forbidden agreement, which removes a key incentive that currently brings generics to market early [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: pay-for-delay deals keep cheaper generic drugs off the market for months or years, and every year of delay is priced into what patients, employers, and Medicare pay. The main cost — losing the ability to settle patent fights with side payments — falls almost entirely on the brand-name drug industry, and the narrow early-entry exception plus FTC exemption authority gives companies a legal path for settlements that genuinely bring generics to market sooner. On balance this is a consumer-protection bill whose costs are borne by the industry being restrained.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees, then to their Health and Intellectual Property subcommittees, and sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush (D-IL), joined by Rep. Henry Waxman, introduced the bill on February 9, 2012 [S1, S3].
The House referred it to both the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees on the day of introduction, a dual referral that requires two committees to act before the bill can move [S5].
Within a week it was further referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Judiciary Subcommittee on Intellectual Property, Competition and the Internet [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote occurred before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies are better off because the bill never advanced: they keep the ability to pay generic challengers to stay off the market, preserving years of monopoly-priced sales that this bill would have cut short. Generic makers that accept those payments also keep the status quo. Consumers who pay drug prices are worse off.

for.name: Rep. Bobby L. Rush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban pay-for-delay settlements and see it referred to committee.

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.what_they_did: Joined Rep. Rush in introducing the bill on the day it was filed.

for.name: 6 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

for.name: Federal Trade Commission
for.role: Federal antitrust enforcer for consumer protection
for.what_they_did: Under the Obama administration, the FTC had challenged pay-for-delay settlements as anticompetitive and endorsed legislation banning them; the bill builds on that enforcement agenda by making the FTC the enforcing agency.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of first referral; Chair, Rep. Fred Upton (R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 9, 2012 and sent it to the Health Subcommittee, where no markup or vote followed.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Second referral committee; Chair, Rep. Lamar Smith (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and sent it to the Subcommittee on Intellectual Property, Competition and the Internet, where no markup or vote followed.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: The brand-drug industry has long opposed federal bans on pay-for-delay settlements, which it defends as ordinary patent litigation settlements.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 6 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill died in committees led by Republicans without reaching a vote.

industries.note: The bill bans the practice by which these companies pay generic challengers to stay off the market, extending years of monopoly-priced sales. Consumers pay higher drug prices as a direct result, so the industry's interest in this bill runs squarely against the public's.

Generic makers gain faster access to markets under the early-entry exception, but lose the 'anything of value' settlements they currently receive for delaying launch, and could lose their 180-day exclusivity reward if they strike a forbidden deal.

industries.industry: Consumers and government drug payers (Medicare, Medicaid, employers)
industries.note: Banning pay-for-delay would bring lower-priced generic versions of drugs to market sooner, lowering what patients and public insurance programs pay.
